Electrolyte preparation The solvent mixtures of DOL/DME (1:1 v/v), DOL/F4DEE (4:1 v/v) and DOL/TTE (4:1 v/v) were prepared in advance.

Four kinds of electrolyte solutions were then prepared: (1) For Li+ solvation study, 1.0 M LiTFSI was dissolved in each single/mixed solvent; (2) For LiPS solvation study, Li2S and S8 were mixed with a molar ratio 8:5 and then dissolved in varied solvents to reach Li2S6 nominal concentration of 0.1 M; (3) For Li||Carbon paper cell construction, 1.0 M LiTFSI and 0.1 M LiNO3 were dissolved in the solutions prepared in (2); (4) For Li||S cell construction, 1.0 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiNO3 were dissolved in varied solvents.

This is because Li+-Sx 2−is much more strongly bonded than Li+-TFSI−, and F4DEE is less capable of coordinating with LiPS than DOL and DME.21 Consequently, the DOL/F4DEE mixed solvent shows a moderate Li2S6 solubility of 0.38 M, in sharp contrast to 1.0 M in DOL/ DME and 0.22 M in DOL/TTE.
The impact of F4DEE on LiPS solvation was evaluated by ultraviolet−visible (UV−vis) spectroscopy (Figure 1e).

The absence of the LiS3 • radical (600 nm) and the decreased intensity of the LiPS absorption peaks (300 and 400 nm) identify the weak LiPS solvating power of DOL/F4DEE.24,28 This is further supported by the intensified LiPS clustering, as shown in the number density distribution of the S6 2−anion around Li+ (Figure 1f).29 The main peak at 2.3 Å implies strong Li+−S6 2−pairing, which is distinctive from the more weakly associated Li+−TFSI−ion pair.

Their increasing peak intensity demonstrates a stronger LiPS clustering tendency, further validating the weak LiPS solvating power of DOL/F4DEE.23 As a result, by introducing PFGstructured F4DEE, the DOL/F4DEE electrolyte boasts high LiTFSI solubility, moderate LiPS solubility, moderate Li+ solvation, and weak LiPS solvation.
The DOL/F4DEE electrolyte possesses a high Li+ conductivity of 3.6 mS cm−1, indicating its capability to facilitate Li+ transport in the bulk electrolyte.
Despite these disparities, all electrolytes in our study possess high Li+ conductivity of > 1.0 mS cm-1, already ensuring fast Li+ transport.
In this work, we decouple the solvation and solubility effects of Li+ and LiPS and correlate them with electrochemical performance through a cosolvent strategy.

By employing a fluorinated−glyme (F-glyme) cosolvent, specifically 1,2-bis(2,2-difluoroethoxy)ethane (F4DEE), that exhibits low LiPS solubility yet moderate Li+ solvation, we designed an electrolyte that enhances lithium anode stability while maintaining sufficient sulfur cathode kinetics, thereby prolonging Li−S cell cycle life.
In this work, we propose a partially fluorinated glyme (Fglyme) cosolvent, 1,2-bis(2,2-difluoroethoxy) ethane (F4DEE), combined with DOL to form a Li−S battery electrolyte.

As a result, the DOL/F4DEE electrolyte features moderate Li+ solvation, moderate LiPS solubility, and weak LiPS solvation, distinguishing it from conventional ether electrolytes (DOL/DME) and F-ether electrolyte (DOL/TTE).
In summary, we present an electrolyte design strategy that achieves a balance between enhanced lithium anode stability and efficient sulfur redox kinetics.
Li||Cu cells were assembled as 2032-coin cells with W-scope separator (single-layer PP) and an electrolyte amount of 50 μL, and were then tested on a Neware BTS4000 battery cycler system.

Li||Cu cells were tested with the Aurbach method, in which a Li plating/stripping formation cycle was first performed at 0.5 mA cm-2 for 10 h, followed by plating the Li reservoir at the same condition.
Then 1 mAh cm-2 Li was stripped/plated for ten cycles before all the Li reservoir was fully stripped at the same current density.

In addition to high Li+ conductivity, the moderate Li+ solvation in DOL/F4DEE enhances the Li stripping/plating stability.

The moderate Li+ solvation in DOL/F4DEE also regulates the stripping/ plating process of the Li anode, showing chunky and dense Li deposition morphology with a relatively reduced Li thickness (Figure 2b, Figure S11).
Thus, the enriched TFSI−anion and F4DEE in the Li+ solvation shell give rise to LiF-rich SEI with the DOL/F4DEE electrolyte.

This LiF-rich SEI enables dense Li deposition morphology, which plays a critical role in achieving high Li plating/stripping CE (Note S3, Figure 2d).35 Moreover, the moderate LiPS solubility in DOL/F4DEE enhances the Li anode cyclability because it confines the concentration of corrosive LiPS in the electrolyte.36 The weak Figure 2.
On the cathode side, weak LiPS solvation thermodynamically favors short-chain LiPS (Li2Sx, x = 2−4) and promotes the oxidation conversion of LiPS to S8 during charging.
This enhances sulfur cathode reversibility and protects the lithium anode from corrosive long-chain LiPS.
LiPS solvation also suppresses parasitic corrosion reactions on the Li metal (Note S4).

Moreover, the retarded LiPS-S8 oxidation accelerates the irreversible consumption of LiNO3.50,51 This is unfavorable for Li−S long-term cycling because LiNO3 is crucial in SEI formation and catalyzing LiPS oxidation.52 Taking these into consideration, weak LiPS solvation in DOL/F4DEE benefits the Li−S battery cycle life despite partially compromised specific capacity.

Notably, its weak LiPS solvation suppresses the formation of corrosive long-chain LiPS and boosts the reversibility of sulfur active material, leading to an enhanced Li−S cycle life (Figure 3c). ■MODERATE LIPS SOLUBILITY IN DOL/F4DEE ENABLES MODERATE CATHODE REDOX KINETICS In addition to LiPS solvation, the electrolyte also determines the soluble LiPS concentration in regular Li−S batteries with carbon/sulfur (C/S) composite cathodes.
Additionally, we illustrate that the small Li−S redox overpotentials correlate with high LiPS solubility owing to facilitated LiPS diffusion.
The moderate LiPS solubility in DOL/F4DEE thus supports fast sulfur redox kinetics, resulting in low cell overpotentials during cycling.
